title: The Reporter’s Recording
subtitle: A leaked audio embarrasses the city; officers want the reporter’s phone
coldOpen: 08:00. A reporter posts audio of a clerk taking a bribe.
09:30. Officers propose seizing her phone “to verify it”.
By ten, a split crowd is outside the Press Club.

briefing.grievance: Residents who paid bribes for building permits want the clerk and the contractor investigated. The clerk’s colleagues say the audio is doctored and the reporter should be arrested.
knownFacts: The audio is 3 minutes long and names a permit clerk and a contractor.
The reporter says she has the original file and a second source.
The clerk was suspended at 09:00 pending inquiry.
unverifiedClaims: A post says the audio was generated by software.
A message says the reporter was paid by a rival contractor.
briefing.responsibility: You run the inquiry and the police liaison. Verify the recording without turning the inquiry into a raid on the press.
briefing.objective: Verify the audio lawfully, protect the reporter and her sources, and investigate the bribe itself.

rightsMoments.question: A reporter published a recording that embarrasses officials. Can her phone be seized to verify it?

options.text: Not as a first step. Verification should use a sealed copy; seizing a journalist’s device exposes sources and needs strict legal process.
options.feedback: Correct. Press freedom includes source protection; any intrusion must be necessary, narrow and lawful.

options.text: Yes. Anyone who publishes evidence must hand over the device it came from.
options.feedback: Publishing evidence does not strip a journalist of legal protections.

options.text: Yes, if officials believe the recording is fake.
options.feedback: A belief that something is fake is tested by examination, not by raids on newsrooms.

rightsMoments.principle: Article 19(1)(a) protects freedom of the press, including the confidentiality of sources. Intrusions must be necessary, proportionate and lawful; verification can be done without them.
rightsMoments.why: The lab verified a sealed copy and found no edits; a raid would have exposed every source on the reporter’s phone for nothing.

simple.question: A reporter posted a recording that embarrasses officials. Can police take her phone to check it?

options.a: Not as a first step. Check a sealed copy. Her sources stay safe.
options.b: Yes. Anyone who posts proof must hand over the device.
options.c: Yes, if officials think it is fake.

feedback.a: Yes! Reporters’ sources are protected. Check a copy instead.
feedback.b: No. Posting proof does not remove a reporter’s rights.
feedback.c: Thinking it is fake is a reason to test it, not to raid.

simple.principle: Reporters are free to report and to protect their sources. Check their proof without raiding them.
simple.why: The lab checked a sealed copy and found no edits. A raid would have exposed every source for nothing.
